L1: # Telegram Widgets
L2: 
L3: Bots can send widgets: small interactive blocks drawn right inside a message. A widget is one self-contained HTML document with inline CSS and JavaScript, at most 32 KB of HTML and 4 KB after compression. Telegram apps run it on the user's device in a sandbox with no network access at all, draw it in the style of the chat, and keep it running while it is on screen: a poll whose bars move as people vote, a price ticker, a board game for two in a group, a promo code that copies on a tap.
L4: A widget is fixed code plus changeable state. The code, its HTML, is set when the widget is sent and never changes. What changes is the widget's state, and only the bot writes it: the chat state, tied to one message and seen only in that chat, and the shared state, seen wherever the widget is shown. The widget reads its state and redraws when it changes. It cannot change the state itself, but it can ask the bot with small requests, the way a callback button does.
L5: Widgets live in the private chat with the bot, in groups, in messages sent via the bot in inline mode, and in forwards to any chat. Currently, in the production environment, widgets work only in the private chat with the bot. The rest works on the 【0†test server】. A widget can also be a shared widget: one widget on the server, like a poll, that any number of messages show, with one shared state for all of them.
L6: This page is a guide to designing and implementing widgets, followed by the reference of the widget's JavaScript object `TelegramWidget`. The Bot API methods and types for widgets are in the 【1†Bot API reference】.
L7: 
L8: * * *
L9: ### Introducing widgets
L10: #### Code and state
L11: 
L12: A widget is fixed code plus changeable state.
L13:   * The code (the HTML with its CSS and JavaScript) is set when the widget is sent and never changes, in a message or in a shared widget. No method replaces it. For a new layout, send a new widget, and old messages keep the old one. As with any media, the caption can be edited.
L14:   * The state is what changes, and only the bot writes it. There are two kinds:
L15:     * chat state (`chat_data`): tied to one message, seen only in that chat (shared by all members in a group), never carried by a forward. A game in progress, whose turn it is.
L16:     * shared state (`public_data`): seen wherever the widget is shown. A static widget keeps it in the message, and a forward gets a copy as of the moment of forwarding. A 【2†shared widget】 (one object with an identifier, like a poll) has one shared state for all its messages and forwards. Poll results, a price.
L17:   * The widget reads its state, learns about changes through the `chatDataChanged` and `publicDataChanged` events, and cannot change its state itself: it can only ask the bot, with a 【3†request】.
L18: Details: 【4†The widget's state】.
L19: #### What a widget is
L20:   * One HTML document. Inline `<style>` and `<script>`, images only as `data:` URLs or inline SVG. At most 32768 bytes of UTF-8 HTML and at most 4096 bytes after the server compresses it with zlib at level 9. The bot sends plain HTML, and the server checks and packs it. A bare fragment without `<html>` and `<body>` works too.
L21:   * Static or shared. A static widget keeps its code and state in the message, and a forward copies them as they are at that moment. A 【2†shared widget】 is one object on the server holding the code, the size, the shared state, the refresh period and the request flag. Any number of messages show it by its identifier, and a change of its shared state reaches all of them.
L22:   * Sandboxed. The widget's JavaScript runs in QuickJS, a small JavaScript engine, never in a WebView or browser context. The client checks every change the widget makes to its page against the 【5†widget profile】 and draws only what passes. The same widget looks the same on iOS, Android, macOS, Telegram Desktop and the web.
L23:   * Offline. `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket` and every other network API throw `NetworkDisabledError`. External scripts, stylesheets, fonts and images are never loaded, and the widget cannot navigate. No library is bundled.
L24:   * Native. The chat's palette is available as CSS variables, and the client's own default styles make a widget without any CSS look like an ordinary message, with buttons in the client's style.
L25:   * Connected through the bot only. The widget's one way out is a request to the bot of up to 64 bytes, which arrives as a 【6†widget_query】 update. The bot's answer goes back to the widget that asked, and only the bot changes the widget's state. The messenger, not the sandbox, carries the traffic.
L26: #### Where widgets live
L27: Where  | How it gets there  | Requests (for a widget sent with `allow_queries`)  | Chat state  | In production
L28: --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
L29: The private chat with the bot  | 【7†sendWidget】  | on a tap, and in the background  | the user's  | Yes
L30: A basic group or supergroup the bot is a member of  | 【7†sendWidget】  | on a tap  | one for all members  | Test server only
L31: Any chat except channels, sent via the bot  | 【8†inline mode】  | on a tap  | per sent message  | Test server only
L32: A forward, in any chat (channels included)  | forwarded by users  | on a tap, only for a 【2†shared widget】  | never  | Test server only
L33: Widgets cannot be posted in channels, directly or via the bot, but users can forward widgets there. Apps that do not support widgets show the message as unsupported media with its caption.
L34: #### Availability
L35: 
L36: Widgets are rolling out in steps. Everything on this page works on the 【9†test server】. Currently, in the production environment, widgets work only in the private chat with the bot.
L37: 
L38: Feature  | Test server  | Production
L39: --- | --- | ---
L40: Widgets in the private chat with the bot, with requests and the wallet  | Yes  | Yes
L41: Forwarding widget messages  | Yes  | No
L42: Widgets in groups  | Yes  | No
L43: Widgets in inline mode  | Yes  | No
L44:   * On the 【9†test server】 every bot can build and test the full set: groups, inline mode and forwards.
L45:   * In the production environment, a bot sends widgets only to private chats with users, and users cannot forward its widget messages. A widget in a private chat that cannot be forwarded has no forwarded copies: design it for that chat alone.
L46: 
L47: The sections below describe the full set. Each section that is not yet in production says so.
L48: #### Widgets and Mini Apps
L49: 
L50: Widgets are not small Mini Apps. A Mini App is a web page you host, opened on demand. A widget is part of the message, always visible as the chat scrolls, and has no network access.
L51: Feature  | Mini Apps  | Widgets
L52: --- | --- | ---
L53: Where  | a web view opened from a button, the menu or a link  | inside the message bubble
L54: Code  | a web page on your server, loaded at launch  | at most 32 KB of HTML inside the message, fixed once created
L55: Engine  | the platform's WebView  | the QuickJS sandbox, with the page changes checked and drawn by the Telegram app
L56: Network  | the web  | none
L57: Talking to the bot  | your own backend, with signed `initData`  | `TelegramWidget.request()`, delivered by Telegram as a `widget_query` or `shared_widget_query` update
L58: State  | your backend, `CloudStorage`, `DeviceStorage`  | the chat state and the shared state, written by the bot, and Web Storage per message on the device
L59: Who is looking  | `initData.user`  | `TelegramWidget.viewer` (id, name, username, Premium), only where the widget may send requests
L60: Input  | everything, keyboard included  | taps, pointer events, horizontal drags and holds, but no keyboard
L61: Where the two APIs overlap, `TelegramWidget` uses the names of `Telegram.WebApp` (`themeParams`, `colorScheme`, `onEvent`, `openLink`, `openTelegramLink`, `HapticFeedback`, `ready`, and `viewer` shaped like `WebAppUser`), so code and habits carry over. For anything larger than a widget, link to your bot or Mini App with `openTelegramLink`.
L62: 
L63: * * *
L64: ### Designing widgets
L65: #### Native look
L66: 
L67: Widgets are drawn on the message bubble, in the chat's colors and text style. Use them instead of your own:
L68:   * The bubble is the canvas. The widget fills the bubble with no padding of its own, and the bubble clips it at its rounded corners. The root element has no background: the bubble's color (`--tg-theme-bg-color`) shows through. A background you set on `html` or `body` paints the whole bubble, up to the rounded edges.
L69:   * Default styles. The app inserts its own default stylesheet beneath yours. Text gets the chat's message color, size and line height. The `body` margin equals the app's text padding (about `8px 12px`), so text starts where a message's text starts. Headings, paragraphs, lists, tables (with separator lines), `pre`, `code`, quotes, links and figure captions get native sizes and margins. Any rule of yours wins over these defaults, whatever its specificity. `body { margin: 0 }` goes edge to edge.
L70:   * Buttons. A `<button>` you do not style is drawn as the client's own button, with a pressed state (`:active`) and a disabled state (`[disabled]`). Your CSS overrides it. It is the only form control: inputs, selects and text areas are removed.
L71:   * The palette is the bubble's. A widget sent by the bot sits in an incoming bubble. A widget the user sent via the bot or forwarded sits in their outgoing bubble, with that bubble's colors. Never hard-code colors that must contrast with the bubble, use the variables instead.

L0: Machine-readable version of this page: /bots/widgets.md.
L1: # Telegram Widgets
L2: 
L3: Bots can send widgets: small interactive blocks drawn right inside a message. A widget is one self-contained HTML document with inline CSS and JavaScript, at most 32 KB of HTML and 4 KB after compression. Telegram apps run it on the user's device in a sandbox with no network access at all, draw it in the style of the chat, and keep it running while it is on screen: a poll whose bars move as people vote, a price ticker, a board game for two in a group, a promo code that copies on a tap.
L4: A widget is fixed code plus changeable state. The code, its HTML, is set when the widget is sent and never changes. What changes is the widget's state, and only the bot writes it: the chat state, tied to one message and seen only in that chat, and the shared state, seen wherever the widget is shown. The widget reads its state and redraws when it changes. It cannot change the state itself, but it can ask the bot with small requests, the way a callback button does.
L5: Widgets live in the private chat with the bot, in groups, in messages sent via the bot in inline mode, and in forwards to any chat. Currently, in the production environment, widgets work only in the private chat with the bot. The rest works on the 【0†test server】. A widget can also be a shared widget: one widget on the server, like a poll, that any number of messages show, with one shared state for all of them.
L6: This page is a guide to designing and implementing widgets, followed by the reference of the widget's JavaScript object `TelegramWidget`. The Bot API methods and types for widgets are in the 【1†Bot API reference】.
L7: 
L8: * * *
L9: ### Introducing widgets
L10: #### Code and state
L11: 
L12: A widget is fixed code plus changeable state.
L13:   * The code (the HTML with its CSS and JavaScript) is set when the widget is sent and never changes, in a message or in a shared widget. No method replaces it. For a new layout, send a new widget, and old messages keep the old one. As with any media, the caption can be edited.
L14:   * The state is what changes, and only the bot writes it. There are two kinds:
L15:     * chat state (`chat_data`): tied to one message, seen only in that chat (shared by all members in a group), never carried by a forward. A game in progress, whose turn it is.
L16:     * shared state (`public_data`): seen wherever the widget is shown. A static widget keeps it in the message, and a forward gets a copy as of the moment of forwarding. A 【2†shared widget】 (one object with an identifier, like a poll) has one shared state for all its messages and forwards. Poll results, a price.
L17:   * The widget reads its state, learns about changes through the `chatDataChanged` and `publicDataChanged` events, and cannot change its state itself: it can only ask the bot, with a 【3†request】.
L18: Details: 【4†The widget's state】.
L19: #### What a widget is
L20:   * One HTML document. Inline `<style>` and `<script>`, images only as `data:` URLs or inline SVG. At most 32768 bytes of UTF-8 HTML and at most 4096 bytes after the server compresses it with zlib at level 9. The bot sends plain HTML, and the server checks and packs it. A bare fragment without `<html>` and `<body>` works too.
L21:   * Static or shared. A static widget keeps its code and state in the message, and a forward copies them as they are at that moment. A 【2†shared widget】 is one object on the server holding the code, the size, the shared state, the refresh period and the request flag. Any number of messages show it by its identifier, and a change of its shared state reaches all of them.
L22:   * Sandboxed. The widget's JavaScript runs in QuickJS, a small JavaScript engine, never in a WebView or browser context. The client checks every change the widget makes to its page against the 【5†widget profile】 and draws only what passes. The same widget looks the same on iOS, Android, macOS, Telegram Desktop and the web.
L23:   * Offline. `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket` and every other network API throw `NetworkDisabledError`. External scripts, stylesheets, fonts and images are never loaded, and the widget cannot navigate. No library is bundled.
L24:   * Native. The chat's palette is available as CSS variables, and the client's own default styles make a widget without any CSS look like an ordinary message, with buttons in the client's style.
L25:   * Connected through the bot only. The widget's one way out is a request to the bot of up to 64 bytes, which arrives as a 【6†widget_query】 update. The bot's answer goes back to the widget that asked, and only the bot changes the widget's state. The messenger, not the sandbox, carries the traffic.
L26: #### Where widgets live
L27: Where  | How it gets there  | Requests (for a widget sent with `allow_queries`)  | Chat state  | In production
L28: --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
L29: The private chat with the bot  | 【7†sendWidget】  | on a tap, and in the background  | the user's  | Yes
L30: A basic group or supergroup the bot is a member of  | 【7†sendWidget】  | on a tap  | one for all members  | Test server only
L31: Any chat except channels, sent via the bot  | 【8†inline mode】  | on a tap  | per sent message  | Test server only
L32: A forward, in any chat (channels included)  | forwarded by users  | on a tap, only for a 【2†shared widget】  | never  | Test server only
L33: Widgets cannot be posted in channels, directly or via the bot, but users can forward widgets there. Apps that do not support widgets show the message as unsupported media with its caption.
L34: #### Availability
L35: 
L36: Widgets are rolling out in steps. Everything on this page works on the 【9†test server】. Currently, in the production environment, widgets work only in the private chat with the bot.
L37: 
L38: Feature  | Test server  | Production
L39: --- | --- | ---
L40: Widgets in the private chat with the bot, with requests and the wallet  | Yes  | Yes
L41: Forwarding widget messages  | Yes  | No
L42: Widgets in groups  | Yes  | No
L43: Widgets in inline mode  | Yes  | No
L44:   * On the 【9†test server】 every bot can build and test the full set: groups, inline mode and forwards.
L45:   * In the production environment, a bot sends widgets only to private chats with users, and users cannot forward its widget messages. A widget in a private chat that cannot be forwarded has no forwarded copies: design it for that chat alone.
L46: 
L47: The sections below describe the full set. Each section that is not yet in production says so.
L48: #### Widgets and Mini Apps
L49: 
L50: Widgets are not small Mini Apps. A Mini App is a web page you host, opened on demand. A widget is part of the message, always visible as the chat scrolls, and has no network access.
L51: Feature  | Mini Apps  | Widgets
L52: --- | --- | ---
L53: Where  | a web view opened from a button, the menu or a link  | inside the message bubble
L54: Code  | a web page on your server, loaded at launch  | at most 32 KB of HTML inside the message, fixed once created
L55: Engine  | the platform's WebView  | the QuickJS sandbox, with the page changes checked and drawn by the Telegram app
L56: Network  | the web  | none
L57: Talking to the bot  | your own backend, with signed `initData`  | `TelegramWidget.request()`, delivered by Telegram as a `widget_query` or `shared_widget_query` update
L58: State  | your backend, `CloudStorage`, `DeviceStorage`  | the chat state and the shared state, written by the bot, and Web Storage per message on the device
L59: Who is looking  | `initData.user`  | `TelegramWidget.viewer` (id, name, username, Premium), only where the widget may send requests
L60: Input  | everything, keyboard included  | taps, pointer events, horizontal drags and holds, but no keyboard
L61: Where the two APIs overlap, `TelegramWidget` uses the names of `Telegram.WebApp` (`themeParams`, `colorScheme`, `onEvent`, `openLink`, `openTelegramLink`, `HapticFeedback`, `ready`, and `viewer` shaped like `WebAppUser`), so code and habits carry over. For anything larger than a widget, link to your bot or Mini App with `openTelegramLink`.
L62: 
L63: * * *
L64: ### Designing widgets
L65: #### Native look
L66: 
L67: Widgets are drawn on the message bubble, in the chat's colors and text style. Use them instead of your own:
L68:   * The bubble is the canvas. The widget fills the bubble with no padding of its own, and the bubble clips it at its rounded corners. The root element has no background: the bubble's color (`--tg-theme-bg-color`) shows through. A background you set on `html` or `body` paints the whole bubble, up to the rounded edges.
L69:   * Default styles. The app inserts its own default stylesheet beneath yours. Text gets the chat's message color, size and line height. The `body` margin equals the app's text padding (about `8px 12px`), so text starts where a message's text starts. Headings, paragraphs, lists, tables (with separator lines), `pre`, `code`, quotes, links and figure captions get native sizes and margins. Any rule of yours wins over these defaults, whatever its specificity. `body { margin: 0 }` goes edge to edge.
L70:   * Buttons. A `<button>` you do not style is drawn as the client's own button, with a pressed state (`:active`) and a disabled state (`[disabled]`). Your CSS overrides it. It is the only form control: inputs, selects and text areas are removed.
L71:   * The palette is the bubble's. A widget sent by the bot sits in an incoming bubble. A widget the user sent via the bot or forwarded sits in their outgoing bubble, with that bubble's colors. Never hard-code colors that must contrast with the bubble, use the variables instead.

item.text: Сейчас последняя версия — Bot API 10.4 от 9 ноября; главная новинка — HTML-виджеты прямо в сообщениях. aiogram 3.31.0 пока поддерживает API 10.3, поэтому покажу вызов через собственный `TelegramMethod`. В обычном Telegram виджеты пока доступны только в личном чате с ботом.

На **10 ноября 2026 года последняя версия — Telegram Bot API 10.4**, выпущенная 9 ноября. Главная новинка — **HTML-виджеты прямо внутри сообщений**, с CSS, JavaScript и возможностью обмениваться данными с ботом. Пока в production они работают только в личных чатах с ботом и недоступны для пересылки. [Официальные изменения](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api#november-9-2026). В **aiogram 3.31.0** пока поддерживается API 10.3, поэтому `sendWidget` вызываем через собственный `TelegramMethod`. Ниже минимальный бот с интерактивным счётчиком. [Changelog aiogram](https://docs.aiogram.dev/en/latest/changelog.html). Установи `aiogram==3.31.0`, задай переменную окружения `BOT_TOKEN`, запусти код и отправь `/widget`: ```python import asyncio import os from aiogram import Bot, Dispatcher, F from aiogram.filters import Command from aiogram.methods.base import TelegramMethod from aiogram.types import Message class SendWidget(TelegramMethod[Message]): __api_method__ = "sendWidget" __returning__ = Message chat_id: int html: str height: int = 120 dp = Dispatcher() @dp.message(Command("widget"), F.chat.type == "private") async def show_widget(message: Message, bot: Bot): await bot(SendWidget( chat_id=message.chat.id, html="""

Нажатий: 0

""", )) async def main(): bot = Bot(token=os.environ["BOT_TOKEN"]) await dp.start_polling(bot) if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) ``` Кнопка меняет содержимое самого сообщения. Здесь счётчик локальный: при пересоздании виджета значение сбросится. Внешние скрипты и сетевые запросы внутри виджета запрещены; для серверных действий предусмотрены `TelegramWidget.request()`, обновления `widget_query` и ответы через `answerWidgetQuery`. [Документация виджетов](https://core.telegram.org/bots/widgets).
